# Modeling Time Series Data
## About Time Series Functions
Time series functions operate on time-oriented dimensions.

To use these functions on a particular dimension, you must designate the dimension as a Time dimension and set one or more keys at one or more levels as chronological keys. These keys identify the chronological order of the members within a dimension level.
### Setting Chronological Keys for Each Level
The Oracle BI Server uses the chronological key to create mathematically correct time series predictions, such as Jan + 2 months = Mar. You should set a chronological key for every level, except for the Grand Total level, so that you can perform time series operations on all levels with good performance. This enables you to use an AGO, TODATE, or PERIODROLLING function for any level of any time dimension hierarchy, such as fiscal month ago, calendar year ago, and day ago.
As with any level key, be sure the key is unique at its level. For example, a column containing simple month names such as "January" is not unique unless it is concatenated to a column containing year names.

# On higher-order averaging of time-periodic systems: reconciliation of two averaging techniques
## Abstract
In this paper we show how higher-order averaging can be used to remedy serious technical issues with the direct application of the averaging theorem. While doing so, we reconcile two higher-order averaging methodologies that were developed independently using different tools and within different communities: (i) perturbation theory using a near-identity transformation and (ii) chronological calculus using Lie algebraic tools. We provide the underpinning concepts behind each averaging approach and provide a mathematical proof for their equivalence up to the fourth order.

Build a Uniswap v2 TWAP oracle using cumulative prices, observation windows, and resilient maintenance patterns.

To build a price oracle on Uniswap v2, you must first understand the requirements for your use case. Once you understand the kind of price average you require, it is a matter of storing the cumulative price variable from the pair as often as necessary, and computing the average price using two or more observations of the cumulative price variables.

## Understanding requirements

To understand your requirements, you should first research the answer to the following questions:

- Is data freshness important? I.e.: must the price average include the current price?
- Are recent prices more important than historical prices? I.e.: is the current price given more weight than historical prices?

Note your answers for the following discussion.

## Fixed windows

In the case where data freshness is not important and recent prices are weighted equally with historical prices, it is enough to store the cumulative price once per period (e.g. once per 24 hours.)

Computing the average price over these data points gives you 'fixed windows', which can be updated after the lapse of each period. We wrote an example oracle of this kind here.

This example does not limit the maximum size of the fixed window, i.e. it only requires that the window size is greater than 1 period (e.g. 24 hours).

In the case where data freshness is important, you can use a sliding window in which the cumulative price variable is measured more often than once per period.

Portfolio risk is not limited to the variance of returns. The moments of portfolio returns depend directly on the covariance matrix and higher-order co-dependences (coskewness, cokurtosis, etc.). In practice, however, these objects are extremely noisy, especially for large portfolios. Here we introduce filtering methods based on tensor decompositions that extend cross-validated covariance cleaning and the Average Oracle methodology to even-order co-moment tensors. The Average Oracle (Bongiorno et al., 2023) follows the same core logic as walk-forward cross-validation; it averages the so-called oracle (i.e., optimal given future data) eigenvalues over many past time windows, which yields a fixed vector of filtered eigenvalues that can be applied to the current window and periodically refreshed if needed. 1.1 Contributions.
Our main contributions lie in the design and analysis of cost-efficient adaptive oracle-switching meta-algorithms, together with concrete stochastic optimization subroutines and LLM experiments.
- • 
Multistage oracle-switching with known bias. We develop a generic meta-algorithm that uses a chosen stochastic optimization subroutine across stages, so that the current squared-distance radius is reduced by a constant factor. At each stage, the policy selects the most cost-efficient oracle for achieving the next contraction among all oracles with admissible bias. As one concrete contraction subroutine, we analyze a strongly convex variant of stochastic gradient extrapolation (SGE) (Lan and Zhou, 2018) under state-dependent noise and persistent bias. For unbiased oracles, the cumulative cost of our framework is no larger than that of the best fixed oracle in hindsight, and the savings can be up to over stages. With biased oracles, the framework can exploit cheaper sources early while ultimately reaching the accuracy scale allowed by lower-bias sources. 
- • 
Characterizing cost with respect to desired accuracy: The stagewise formulation yields explicit operational criteria for comparing oracle cost and fidelity. We characterize when one oracle is dominated by another and derive stage-dependent break-even prices that quantify how much one should be willing to pay for a higher-fidelity source at a given downstream accuracy level.

Walk-forward analysis repeatedly trains a model on historical data, evaluates it on a later window, then advances the timeline and repeats the process. For example, a researcher might train on an earlier period, test on the following period, and retrain using information available before the next test window. Portfolio risk is not limited to the variance of returns. The moments of portfolio returns depend directly on the covariance matrix and higher-order co-dependences (coskewness, cokurtosis, etc.). In practice, however, these objects are extremely noisy, especially for large portfolios. Here we introduce filtering methods based on tensor decompositions that extend cross-validated covariance cleaning and the Average Oracle methodology to even-order co-moment tensors. Using returns on historical Russell 1000 constituents, we find that the proposed filters improve out-of-sample estimation accuracy relative to sample estimators, both for correlation and cokurtosis tensors, as measured by relative squared Frobenius errors.

The Average Oracle (Bongiorno et al., 2023) follows the same core logic as walk-forward cross-validation; it averages the so-called oracle (i.e., optimal given future data) eigenvalues over many past time windows, which yields a fixed vector of filtered eigenvalues that can be applied to the current window and periodically refreshed if needed. This additional averaging acts as a regularizer against regime-specific fluctuations and, in empirical evaluations, systematically delivers more accurate covariance estimates than methods relying solely on the most recent data Bongiorno and Challet (2024).

webiq.snippet: Walk-forward validation is a rigorous method for testing trading strategies that partitions historical data into a sequence of training and testing windows, solving the overoptimization problem endemic to standard backtesting. Unlike in-sample optimization, which allows parameter estimates to exploit random historical coincidence, walk-forward testing constrains a strategy to the same out-of-sample evidence that a real trader encounters, producing performance estimates closer to live trading results. The approach requires reoptimizing parameters at regular intervals and validating the reoptimized strategy on forward-unseen data, enforcing a practical discipline: a strategy's rules are fixed before each test period begins. ... Walk-forward validation addresses this by enforcing a constraint: do not optimize on the same data you test on. Instead, divide the historical record into a series of overlapping or adjacent windows. Optimize parameters using only the first window (the "training set" or "in-sample" period). Evaluate the resulting strategy on the immediately following window (the "test set" or "out-of-sample" period) that the optimization never saw. When that test period ends, move forward, reoptimize on a new training window, and test on the next forward period. Repeat this cycle across the entire historical span.  ... Suppose historical data spans January 2000 to December 2019. A trader might use a 3-year training window and a 1-year test window, stepping forward by 1 year. The first training set is January 2000 to December 2002. The first test set is January 2003 to December 2003. After the test period ends, the training window advances: the second training set is January 2001 to December 2003, and the second test set is January 2004 to December 2004. This continues forward. ... From 2005 to 2015, a researcher might conduct a 10-year walk-forward test with 2-year training windows and 1-year test windows, advancing 1 year at a time.
